entries.title: Cash floods CPS School Board races, with big money groups outraising the Chicago Teachers Union 5 to 1
entries.summary: <p>Back when the idea of an elected school board was still being debated, opponents voiced fears that the powerful Chicago Teachers Union would simply try to buy the elections.</p><p>Yet as Chicago stands on a historic precipice of electing all<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/" target="_blank" ><u> 20 members and a citywide president</u></a> on Nov. 3 that’s not how it’s playing out.</p><p>Cash is flooding the election but the bulk<b> </b>so far has come from wealthy, often suburban donors, whose political groups have outraised the CTU five to 1 and outspent the teachers union nearly three to 1, according to an analysis of the most recent campaign finance filings between Oct. 1, 2025 and Oct. 15, 2026.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-6e0000" name="html-embed-module-6e0000"></a><div style="min-height:311px" id="datawrapper-vis-LhB6K"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/LhB6K/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-LhB6K"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/LhB6K/full.png" alt="A bar chart with four blue bars of different lengths. The headline reads, “Spending by PACs and super PACs”. The description below reads, “Money that has gone to support or oppose CPS School Board candidates between Oct. 1, 2025 and Oct. 15, 2026”. The bars are sorted from longest to shortest, and each one’s length indicates a dollar amount. At the top, the first bar is nearly double the length of the next. That top bar is labeled “Common Ground Collective” and lists an amount of $3.81 million. Below it is a bar for “Illinois Network of Charter Schools” and an amount of $2.08 million. Next, in a bar that is roughly halved yet again in length from the one before, is “Chicago Teachers Union” with $0.92 million. And below that, slightly shorter, is “Service Employees International Union” with $0.69 million." /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>Charter school backers and a few prominent billionaires aligned in a shared antipathy for the teachers union have aimed their millions attacking the Chicago Teacher Union’s choice for board president rather than at bolstering any particular candidate, the Sun-Times/WBEZ analysis shows.</p><p>More than a quarter<b> </b>of the $8.1 million total<b> </b>spent on all races so far by these political action committees and the independent expenditure committees, known as super PACs, has targeted a single candidate: <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/candidates/hilario-dominguez/" target="_blank" ><u>Hilario Dominguez</u></a>.</p><p>The spending to oppose Dominguez is more than four times the amount spent on the top supported candidate, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/candidates/jessica-biggs/" target="_blank" ><u>Jessica Biggs</u></a>, one of the other two candidates for school board president.</p><p>Biggs, a former CPS principal, has attracted wide-ranging contributions from labor unions other than the CTU, former CPS leaders and investment bankers and CEOs — such as Michael Sacks of GCM Grosvenor and Paul Finnegan of Madison Dearborn Partners.</p><p>Both Biggs and Dominguez have directly raised about $1 million. Defense attorney <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/candidates/victor-p-henderson/" target="_blank" ><u>Victor Henderson</u></a>, who lent himself $500,000, trails in fundraising with no support from special interest groups, unions or PACs — <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/10/14/4-takeaways-from-cps-school-board-president-forum" target="_blank" ><u>something he touts</u></a>.</p><p>Arnie Rivera, CPS former chief operating officer<b> </b>who heads a new advocacy group called the Chicago Education Alliance, says the billionaire-funded political groups see the school board races as an opportunity to take down the CTU ahead of the mayoral race in February. Mayor Brandon Johnson remains closely allied with the union, which helped catapult their former organizer to office. Some of the $12.7 million raised by three education-focused political action committees currently spending big will almost certainly be deployed in the mayor’s race.</p><p>“It just becomes a proxy battle on the political side,” Rivera says. “CTU is a huge political group here in the city, and I think you have people who are trying to push back on it. I think that is what it comes down to.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-980000" name="html-embed-module-980000"></a><div style="min-height:611px" id="datawrapper-vis-VDJ4k"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/VDJ4k/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-VDJ4k"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/VDJ4k/full.png" alt="A chart with five rectangles, all stacked vertically in one column together. A headline reads, “CTU-endorsed candidate for board president is the main target of PAC spending”. The description below it says, “Powerful outside groups have spent about $8.1 million on the school board election so far. More than a quarter has gone to oppose Hilario Dominguez, the Chicago Teachers Union’s pick for president.” The chart’s top two rectangles are different shades of orange, and the bottom three are different shades of gray; a thick black line separates the orange section from the gray section. Above the chart is a label: “Spending by political action committees and Super PACs, in millions of dollars”. The orange rectangles represent spending in opposition of particular candidates, and together they take up about two-fifths of the chart’s overall height. The gray rectangles represent spending in support of particular candidates, and together they take up the other three-fifths or so of the chart’s overall height. The topmost portion of the chart is a brightly colored orange rectangle showing $2.30 million spent opposing Hilario Dominguez; below that is a light orange rectangle showing $0.98 million spent opposing candidates for board member or president other than Dominguez. In the gray section, looking from the other end, there is a small, dark gray rectangle showing $0.58 million spent supporting Dominguez, followed by a similarly sized and lighter gray rectangle showing $0.53 million spent supporting Jessica Biggs. Above those (so in the middle between them and the orange opposition spending) is a large, light gray rectangle showing $3.79 million spent supporting candidates for board member or president other than Dominguez or Biggs." /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>The latest campaign finance reports from the Illinois State Board of Elections, which were due by midnight Thursday, show an escalation of cash and spending in the last three months, both directly by the campaigns, as well as by outside groups on their behalf.</p><p>The 43 total candidates vying for board seats have directly raised another $4.1 million since the end of June, adding up to $5.9 million in contributions since October 2025. Since August, four candidates have withdrawn. There are also four write-in candidates.</p><p>Candidates just for the board president position account for $3.5 million,<b> </b>including contributions for two who recently dropped out.</p><p>Twenty local district races, 15 of which are contested, split the remaining $2.4 million. Eleven races have accumulated more than $100,000, with one <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/school-board/districts/1b/" target="_blank" ><u>competitive Northwest Side race in District 1b</u></a> pulling in $292,062 in contributions.</p><p>None of the five district candidates running unopposed are aligned with the CTU. Current school board members <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/candidates/che-rhymefest-smith/" target="_blank" ><u>Che “Rhymefest” Smith</u></a> and <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/elections/2026/graphics/chicago-school-board-education-voter-guide/school-board/districts/4b/" target="_blank" ><u>Ellen Rosenfeld</u></a> have raised $100,000 each.</p><p>“I'm open to taking money from anybody,” Smith says, noting that he also has gotten donations from SEIU, the union that represents support staff in CPS. “But I'll tell you one thing that's interesting: they never asked me to vote a certain way. </div><p></p><h4><b>Big money coming from a new outside group</b></h4><p>The real money in these races is being raised and spent outside the campaigns via a series of political action committees and The latter face no limits on how much they can raise or spend, as long as they don’t coordinate with candidates.</p><p>In addition to wealthy charter school supporters who typically amass and spend<b> </b>when school issues are at stake, billionaire Sacks has dropped millions attacking the Chicago Teachers Union candidates via his newly formed Common Ground Collective super PAC.</p><p>That group has spent the most so far, $3.7 million on digital ads and production, about half of it attacking Dominguez, a teacher-turned-CTU deputy political director.</p><p>The group has yet to endorse or fund ads in support of anyone for board president, though Sacks himself gave $400,000 to Biggs earlier this month.</p><p><a class="Link" undercut Chicago Teachers Union candidates. He has donated $5.5 million to groups involved with the school board election.</p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Sun-Times file</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Close on his heels with $3.8 million is Jim Frank, a retired executive from Winnetka<b>, </b>and regular major donor to the Illinois Network of Charter Schools’ political spending groups.</p><p>The INCS Action super PAC has spent $450,000 on a digital ad opposing Dominguez, but only $1,000 supporting one candidate for president who has since dropped out.<b> </b>INCS’ political arms have not made any endorsement for president.</p><p>Outspent by the CTU in 2024, the INCS Action groups have also spent an additional $1.7 million supporting 19 candidates currently in board races,<b> </b>including to candidates who face no opponent.</p><p>Representatives from Common Ground Collective and INCS declined interview requests.</p><p>Dominguez says money isn’t everything.</p><p>“What I'll say is this — that we didn't go from mayoral control to go to billionaire control, right?” Dominguez says. “At no point in this race did we think we were going to be beating billionaires in spending money. One thing that we've seen and we're seeing across the entire country is that organized people beats organized money any day of the week.”</p><h4>Spending big to make a splash </h4><p>The third group aligned in this election against the teachers union is The Urban Center, though its donations and spending are dwarfed by INCS and the Common Ground Collective.</p><p>Juan Rangel, the executive director of the center, which promotes school choice across public and private schools, said if you want to make an impact, you need to spend big money. That requires first educating people that a school board race is happening and explaining what’s at stake.</p><p>“I would hope that people would understand that these school board elections are the most important races on the November ballot, and they will have implications and ramifications to the February mayoral election," Rangel says.</p><p>What’s different about Chicago is that the wealthy billionaires are local, rather than outsiders pushing a conservative agenda, says Jeffrey R. Henig, a professor emeritus at Columbia University's Teachers College, who co-wrote the book, “Outside Money in School Board Elections: The Nationalization of Education Politics.”</p><p>“I'm struck by … the lack of sharp ideological cleavages and the relative absence of the culture war politics that you see in a lot of suburban districts,” he says. For example, no one is pushing book bans.</p><p>He also points out differences between candidates are more subtle than in ones where big national social issues are at play, so “instead of eliminating charter schools in Chicago, it's about how and under what extreme circumstances we might close some schools.”</p><p>Teacher unions usually enjoy a built-in advantage, regardless of money, Henig says. That’s because teachers and parents with a vested interest in what happens in schools are the most likely to show up and actually vote in school board elections.</p><h3>Is CTU spending coming?</h3><p>The CTU ended up outspending everyone else two years ago — $4.3 million via two political action committees, with about half dropping in the last month.</p><p>It’s been slower so far this time in unrolling campaign ads.</p><p>The CTU has disclosed raising about $2.5 million and spent about $2.2 million through its political organization as well as Our Schools PAC, which it funds.</p><p>“What is unusual in spending in a race is spending a tremendous amount of money not for somebody for president but against somebody,” says CTU Pavlyn Jankov, the union’s research director.</p><p>“We’re never going to compete with the billionaires in this race, and our members support our candidates, so we're going to be continuing to put our money into this race because it reflects the values of 30,000 members.”</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-580000" name="html-embed-module-580000"></a><div style="min-height:353px" id="datawrapper-vis-Gg4nH"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/Gg4nH/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-Gg4nH"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/Gg4nH/full.png" alt="A column chart with four columns, each representing a dollar amount spent in a given month. The headline reads, “How the Chicago Teachers Union rolled out its political spending in 2024”. The description below reads, “Spending by CTU’s political action committee and related PACs on school board races in first school board election, by month”. Below that, the chart shows a column (i.e., a bar stretching vertically) for each month from August through November 2024. The first two (August and September) are much shorter than the remaining two (October and November). August 2024 has an amount of about $164,100. September has an amount of about $301,700. October has an amount (again, much larger than the preceding one) of $1.7 million. November has the slightly smaller amount of $1.6 million." /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>More contributions and spending still could come. Like most labor unions, its coffers get replenished through member dues. CTU leaders tried in vain last spring to get members to increase dues, which could have gone toward political spending.</p><p>Robert Bruno, director of the University of Illinois Urbana-Champaign’ labor education department and author of a book about the 2012 CTU strike, says the union’s resources have been stretched lately, by <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/08/17/chicago-teachers-union-illinois-policy-institute-defamation-lawsuit-stacy-davis-gates" target="_blank" ><u>lawsuits</u></a> as well as <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2025/11/25/ctu-to-cooperate-with-congressional-inquiry-over-financial-audits-chicago-teachers-union" target="_blank" ><u>federal probes</u> — and other elections.</a></p><p>“I can't help but also acknowledge that in addition to this first-ever school board race, there's also the mayoral race, and there's a lot of competition. And that competition involves candidates who have raised a fair amount of money, can raise a lot of money, and obviously, if Mayor Johnson's going to get reelected, he's going to need a very, very highly engaged and supportive Chicago Teachers Union.”</p><p>Plus, he notes, Biggs is no enemy to labor, squarely backed by SEIU.</p><h4>The CTU-SEIU union split</h4><p>Another factor in this election is that the SEIU, the union that represents support staff, has split from its once-close ally, the CTU, after accusing the teachers union of trying to raid some of their members. And they’ve split on most of their candidate endorsements, parting ways on 10 endorsements, including board president. They only overlap on five endorsements</p><p>But Anthony Driver, the chair of a new SEIU-funded PAC Brighter Futures, warned against lumping his union with the other political groups that are anti-CTU.</p><p>“We are not a corporate PAC,” he says. “If anything we are a PAC that operates similarly to the CTU.”</p><p>“We represent low wage workers who are largely erased,” he says, “and it entries.title: 4 Chicago area congressional offices receive suspicious letters amid wave of preelection threats
entries.summary: <p>The offices of four Democratic state representatives each received suspicious letters Friday. </p><p>Reps. Brad Schneider, Mike Quigley, Robin Kelly and Jan Schakowsky reported being sent the letters in a broader wave of threatening packages mailed to congressional and state election offices nationwide ahead of Election Day in November. </p><p>The reports come as <a class="Link" href="https://www.npr.org/2026/10/15/nx-s1-6003857/suspicious-mailings-election-congressional-offices" target="_blank" >similar suspicious mail</a> has been sent to election officials and representatives in several states, including Louisiana, Ohio and Oklahoma, NPR reported.</p><p>Schneider’s office, which is located in Linconshire, contacted Lincolnshire and U.S. Capitol police after receiving the suspicious letter. It was ultimately deemed to not contain harmful substances by law enforcement.</p><p>Quigley’s office at 1925 N. Clybourn Ave. was also evacuated as a precaution Friday when a suspicious letter arrived there. Schakowsky's Skokie office didn't open the letter after warnings from the House sergeant-at-arms.</p><p>Schneider said the FBI is looking into the rash of threatening letters. The bureau didn’t immediately respond to a request for details on the investigation.</p><p>"It is imperative that [the FBI] follow all leads to apprehend and prosecute those responsible,” Schneider said in a statement. "Anyone or any group who thinks they can scare or intimidate Members of Congress or our teams from doing our job and work on behalf of the people we represent is sorely mistaken."</p><p>Kelly said her team immediately contacted the U.S. Capitol Police, which she said is also investigating the incident. The police force didn't immediately respond to requests for comment.</p><p>The Illinois State Board of Elections <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/10/15/feds-investigating-suspicious-letter-sent-to-chicago-election-office" target="_blank" ><u>evacuated its offices</u></a> Thursday when it received a suspicious letter, which was taken as part of the investigation by the FBI. A similar<a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/15/envelope-suspicious-substance-maria-pappas-cook-county-fbi" target="_blank" ><u> suspicious envelope</u></a> containing baking powder was delivered to Cook County Treasurer Maria Pappas’ downtown office at 118 N. Clark St. also on Thursday.</p><p>“Political violence has no place in a democracy, and efforts to scare or intimidate the public in the lead-up to an election must be resoundingly condemned,” Quigley said in a statement. “I hope that the perpetrator is swiftly brought to justice.”</p><div class="RelatedList Enhancement" data-module data-align-center> <div class="RelatedList-title">Related</div> <ul class="RelatedList-items"> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/10/15/feds-investigating-suspicious-letter-sent-to-chicago-election-office" >Feds investigating ‘suspicious’ letter sent to Chicago election office</a> </li> <li class="RelatedList-items-item"> <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/15/envelope-suspicious-substance-maria-pappas-cook-county-fbi" >Pappas office receives envelope with ‘suspicious’ substance, turns out to be baking powder</a> </li> </ul> </div> <p></p>

entries.title: Insufficient evidence that Chicago School Board candidate engaged in sexual misconduct, watchdog report finds
entries.summary: <p>Chicago Public Schools’ watchdog determined there was insufficient evidence that Hilario Dominguez, a candidate for Chicago School Board president, engaged in sexual misconduct with a CPS student nearly a decade ago, in part because there were no eyewitnesses to the alleged behavior and her allegations did not point to a “sustained pattern of behavior.”</p><p>The 34-page report, obtained by WBEZ Friday through an open records request, notes that when the inspector general’s office first opened its case in 2021, it did so because CPS was notified that a Pilsen-based nonprofit had investigated Dominguez in 2018 for alleged conduct “that raised grooming concerns.”</p><p>But after interviewing the young woman who raised the allegations, investigators said the two incidents she recalled that made her feel uncomfortable in 2017, when she was 17 years old, were “less indicative of sexual misconduct” and “narrower in scope” than the internal report filed with the nonprofit.</p><p>The inspector general’s office said the woman alleged that Dominguez asked “about her dating preferences on one occasion” and physically picked her up “holding her body against his, and swinging her from side to side on another occasion.” After she complained to staff at The Resurrection Project, the nonprofit where she participated in a summer jobs program, Dominguez “never made her uncomfortable again.”</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/10/09/reopened-probe-into-cps-board-president-candidates-alleged-inappropriate-contact-with-teen-could-end-soon" target="_blank" ><u>The reopened investigation</u></a>, coming just weeks before voters head to the polls, <a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/10/14/cps-watchdog-closes-investigation-of-school-board-candidate-with-no-actionable-finding-of-sexual-misconduct" target="_blank" ><u>has roiled the heated race for school board president</u></a>. Dominguez, a former CPS teacher and former deputy political director for the Chicago Teachers Union, has denied the allegations and said they were surfaced by Aida Flores, a former political opponent who ran against him for a City Council seat in 2019.</p><p>The inspector general’s office said the upcoming election was not a factor in reopening the investigation, and that the young woman did not seem to have a political motive to first report the alleged behavior to The Resurrection Project in 2017.</p><p>The CPS watchdog reopened its investigation last month after the young woman, who is now 26, called that office and said she hadn’t known about the investigation and wanted a chance to speak with investigators.</p><p>“The political backdrop is relevant but should not distract from the question at the heart of this investigation: whether Dominguez attempted to groom [redacted name] for a sexual purpose or sexually harassed her,” the report states. “Given that those allegations were not otherwise corroborated by the evidence, the OIG did not have to consider the issue of political motivation to determine that the allegations against Dominguez are not substantiated.”</p><p>If the incidents did happen, the inspector general’s office wrote, it was also unclear if they were sexually motivated. The office said it’s possible the behavior the young woman described could have been “part of an ill-advised matchmaking effort or attempt to relate to her as a mentor.”</p><p>And while the alleged conduct, alongside the available evidence, didn’t meet the school district’s threshold for grooming or sexual harassment, the inspector general’s office said the alleged conduct would not be acceptable for a CPS staffer and noted that it would violate CPS’ current standards for boundaries between staff and students.</p><p>But those standards did not yet exist in 2017 and Dominguez was on a break from working at CPS at the time.</p><p>Earlier this week, Rima Kapitan, a lawyer for Dominguez, said the inspector general’s report “fully cleared” Dominguez of any wrongdoing.</p><p>Dominguez <a class="Link" href="https://hilarioforcps.com/with-office-of-inspector-general-investigation-announcing-he-is-cleared-in-full-hilario-dominguez-recenters-race-on-competing-visions/" target="_blank" ><u>said in a statement on Wednesday</u></a> that he now wants to “re-center his campaign” on education issues.</p><p>In a statement provided to WBEZ through her lawyer, the young woman said the process for investigating her claims had been “deeply flawed.”</p><p>“Like so many victims and survivors undermined by a broken system before me, I know what happened to me, and I am not going to be silenced,” she wrote. “While I am disappointed in the failure of this report to affirmatively verify my experience, it certainly does not exonerate Hilario Dominguez, or ‘clear him in full,’ as he claims.”</p><p>The inspector general’s office attempted to reach the young woman and her parents on 12 occasions in 2022, including leaving several voicemails for her mother and father as well as direct messages to the woman’s social media accounts, according to the report. It adds that the woman’s mother “would have been familiar with the OIG and would have been trained” on sexual misconduct investigation practices within CPS.</p><p>Additionally, investigators reviewed text messages that were “potentially inconsistent” with some of the young woman’s claims. She told the inspector general’s office that Dominguez had reached out to her on two occasions to set up a meeting in 2020 and 2022.</p><p>However, text messages show that it was the young woman, not Dominguez, who reached out for a meeting in 2022, including suggesting they meet alone. The meeting never took place.</p><p>The report adds that the potential inconsistencies could exist because the exchanges took place a long time ago.</p><p>In a statement Friday, Inspector General Philip Wagenknecht stressed that his office is apolitical and that its investigation began long before the school board president race kicked off this year. He said the investigation was in “no way” rushed or “concluded prematurely.”</p><p>“No one outside this office has influence over how OIG investigations are handled, and there were no external efforts to influence this matter,” he wrote.</p><p>The report cited “heavy caseload and limited resources” for the reason that it took five years to close the initial investigation.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://www.wbez.org/education/2026/10/14/cps-watchdog-closes-investigation-of-school-board-candidate-with-no-actionable-finding-of-sexual-misconduct" target="_blank" ><u>The young woman’s lawyer sent letters Wednesday</u></a> to the inspector general, CPS board members and the district’s superintendent calling for an independent review of how the inspector general’s office investigated this case.</p><p>Sixteen City Council members also called for an independent investigation Thursday, claiming the process was “tainted.”</p><p>“The Mayor’s hand-picked CPS Inspector General rushed a finding to meet the deadline he publicly demanded, sending a devastating message to every girl weighing whether to report abuse,” the members said in a statement.</p><p>A spokesperson for the mayor’s office said that “at no point” did it contact the inspector general’s office during its investigation or “make any attempt” to exert influence.</p><p><i>Contributing: Sarah Karp</i></p><div entries.title: Six months after the Sky traded her away, Angel Reese is in the WNBA Finals
entries.summary: <p>SAN FRANCISCO — The thing that I’ve always found spookiest about former <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/chicago-sky" target="_blank" ><u>Sky</u></a> star Angel Reese is the way she speaks things into existence.</p><p>She’d put pretty much every accomplishment this year — from making the FIBA World Cup team to being named Defensive Player of the Year to reaching her first WNBA Finals — out into the universe well beforehand.</p><p>She calls it manifesting.</p><p>I remember being caught off guard by her manifesting last season, when she casually dropped in a pregame interview that she was planning on becoming Defensive Player of the Year. I’d always thought of her as a good, instinctive defender, but she, at 23 years old, thought she could dethrone the likes of A’ja Wilson and Napheesa Collier?</p><p>She could and she did. Impressive stuff.</p><p>But what I most enjoyed about covering Reese, in the two years before the Sky traded her to the Dream, was the way she made you think. My questions about her ranged from the little mysteries to the big ones.</p><p>Little: Why could she outjump anybody for a rebound, but when she shot a layup, seemed to dive toward the rim and windshield-wiper the ball up?</p><p>Big: What made her work so ravenously toward her goals? Would she ever view life as something other than a set of stages to be conquered? Would she look back the way she looks forward?</p><p>I asked her about this Friday, on the eve of Game 1 in San Francisco, reminding her that as a rookie, she once told us that she didn’t really ever have time to reflect. Now that she was in a slightly different moment in her life, had that changed? Her answer was basically no.</p><p>“I think my journey speaks for itself,” she said. “A year ago I was walking in [the Victoria's Secret fashion show] for the first time ever. Now a year later I’m on the biggest stage and being able to be in the Finals.</p><p>“I haven’t had time to really reflect yet. Maybe the offseason is time, but I always have something going on in the off season, so it’s really hard.</p><p>“But I think like: I work hard now in my 20s, my early 30s so I can rest and relax and have a family and do all the other fun things when I’m older.”</p><p>Fair enough: she can leave the reflecting to the writers and the old folk while she marches on.</p><p>I still think about Reese’s time in Chicago often. I can picture waking up to the subject heading in my inbox on that fateful Monday in April: “Chicago Sky Trade Angel Reese to the Atlanta Dream, Acquire Draft Picks.”</p><p>I groaned. It was <i>just</i> like the Sky to recognize her potential while others doubted her, trade valuable draft capital to get her, and then fail to make it work long-term.</p><p>I knew Reese’s short tenure was a huge opportunity blown for the franchise, and that her departure would hurt fans. Personally, though, I was ambivalent. I’d miss her booming presence, but I was glad to be done with the mess of haters and rabid defenders around her. With the Sky in such a steep decline, I wasn’t sure any one player could turn things around.</p><p>When I sat down to write, the first thing that came to mind was the story of Jack and the Beanstalk. The protagonist, Jack, is sent by his family to sell their cow, but to their dismay, Jack returns with a bag of magic beans.</p><p><i>The Sky traded forward Angel Reese to the Dream on Monday for a bag of magic beans,</i> I wrote. That may have captured how fans felt in the moment, but it wasn’t totally accurate — in the English fairy tale, the beans actually end up saving Jack’s family. In this story, they won’t. The only immediate return the Sky will get from the Dream this offseason is the No. 12 pick in the 2027 draft. The last time the Sky drafted that late in the first round, they ended up with the not-exactly-franchise-changing services of Hailey Van Lith.</p><p>The best hope for the Sky is that the “beans” grow into a lesson: if you trade up to draft an alpha star like Reese, you need a robust plan to see it through.</p><p>What Reese has taught me is that great players change your understanding of what, exactly, greatness looks like. I thought her layup form might limit her, but I was wrong. She’s now anchoring a Finals team, averaging 18 points and 8 rebounds in the playoffs. She’s doing it with her motor, IQ and, surprisingly, more confidence from three.</p><p>A good reminder to weigh a player’s mindset and desire just as heavily as their form.</p>

entries.title: Nic Claxton expected to be only Bull not available to start season
entries.summary: <p>The Bulls will be close to 100% healthy when they open the season Wednesday at the Raptors. Only center Nic Claxton, who’s nursing a hamstring injury, won’t be ready. But coach Tiago Splitter said the seven-year veteran is ramping up basketball activities.</p><p>“Every day he does something else and more aggressive,” Splitter said Friday before the Bulls’ preseason finale against the Timberwolves. “But — I’m not going to stop repeating this — this is a very dangerous injury. The chances of redoing it are big. So we’ve got to be careful.”</p><p>Claxton suffered the injury during a training-camp practice early this month. He and center Zach Collins (quad) were seen working out during the morning shootaround at the Advocate Center, Claxton jogging lightly and Collins jumping rope.</p><p>“[Collins is] supposed to be 100%,” Splitter said. “He’s supposed to be in all the practices that we have left. Full contact, everything.”</p><p>Forward Tobe Awaka and guard Isaac Okoro have been out with knee injuries. They joined Collins and Claxton on the sideline Friday.</p><p>Splitter went into the game looking for improvement in several areas.</p><p>“I can give you a list,” he said. “We got to rebound better; we got to take care of the ball; we got to crash more on offense; the ball cannot stick, we got to move the ball side to side. Those are the most important things right now.”</p><p>When Splitter has everyone available, he expects to have a nine-to-10-man rotation most of the time because he wants the Bulls to run.</p><h3>Giddey’s a video star</h3><p>He isn’t yet the “Czar of the Telestrator,” the nickname of former NBA coach and TV analyst Mike Fratello, but Bulls guard Josh Giddey is breaking down game video of himself on his YouTube channel, @OfficialJoshGiddey. He has four videos up and many more to come. Giddey plans to post one every Sunday night.</p><p>“I saw Tom Brady do it on a football game from a quarterback’s perspective,” Giddey said. “I love watching football and the NFL, and I never really understood it on that deep a level. It was really cool to see, and I thought that’s something I could do for basketball.”</p><p>Giddey is a video junkie. Since he’s watching anyway, he figured why not teach fans how he sees the game as a point guard. He takes videos of himself, then sends them to editors who combine his video with the game video and add graphic elements. Giddey’s first video, which posted Sept. 20, was about his game-winning halfcourt shot to beat the Lakers last season.</p><p>“I’ve always loved when top-tier athletes, whatever sport they’re in, have broken it down on a pretty deep level,” said Giddey, who has more than 20,000 subscribers. “It gives fans a better understanding of the game.”</p><h3>Is it Miller’s time?</h3><p>Forward Leonard Miller entered Friday leading the Bulls in preseason scoring with 17.5 points per game. Splitter has been impressed, but he said Miller has more to prove.</p><p>“He’s a mismatch for slower fives,” Splitter said. “We can use him in that position; we can use him at the four position. He’s playing well so far.</p><p>“It’s still only the preseason. Wednesday, when the lights are on, it’s going to be a different game. You’ve got to also think about that.”</p><h3>Time change</h3><p>The Bulls’ game next Friday at the Bucks was moved to 3 p.m. from 7 because it would’ve conflicted with Game 1 of the World Series, which will be in Milwaukee.</p>

entries.title: Jake Nawrot and Jackson Travis help Hersey pile up more than 600 yards to beat Prospect
entries.summary: <p>The focus for opposing defenses when playing No. 5 Hersey this season has been on quarterback Jake Nawrot, and rightfully so.</p><p>The 6-4, 200-pound senior is a four-star prospect committed to Kentucky. He's the consensus No. 5 quarterback and No. 65 player nationally in his class.</p><p>Nawrot hasn't put up the gaudiest stat line this fall, partly because the Huskies had a forfeit win against Wheeling and haven't had to play their starters much after halftime.</p><p>But in the rivalry game Friday night at No. 13 Prospect, Hersey needed all the offense it could muster. Nawrot delivered, and so did junior running back Jackson Travis. The Huskies piled up more than 600 yards en route to a 48-35 win before a standing-room-only crowd.</p><p>Nawrot was 23 of 27 passing for 326 yards for four touchdowns, three of them to Josh Riggs. Travis ran 36 times for a program-record 294 yards and two touchdowns, including a 59-yarder. Nawrot also ran for a short TD.</p><p>"It shows that we can do it on the ground and in the air," Nawrot said. "I don't care what the stats are. It just showed that wherever the ball was, the one-yard line or ... the 50 — we can go and punch it in no matter what. It's a testament to the work we put in in practice and our preparation."</p><p>The Huskies (9-0, 5-0 Mid-Suburban East) leaned hard on Travis after halftime, when he had 22 carries for 236 yards as they worked the clock.</p><p>"For this game, I want to give all my credit to the O-line," he said. "They had almost the perfect game. I give all my credit to them, but I think we really came together as a team, really executed it perfectly."</p><p>"He's a beast," Hersey coach Tom Nelson said of Travis. "A lot of the games we played, we only played [the starters] two quarters, so the stat line might not show it. But I'm super happy for him."</p><p>That feeling extended to the passing game, too, for obvious reasons.</p><p>"One of the big things that is a strength of ours offensively is we have balance," Nelson said. "We use all five eligible players — run, throw, whatever they want to give us, we're happy to take it."</p><p>Nawrot completed passes to seven receivers, with Riggs leading the way with six catches for 105 yards. Jaxon St. Paul had five receptions for 75 yards and Dom Wentink had the other touchdown catch, a 51-yarder.</p><p>Hersey never trailed in a game that turned into a track meet after halftime, when both teams scored 28 points.</p><p>Prospect (8-1, 4-1) stayed within striking distance by piling up some big numbers of its own.</p><p>Knights quarterback Jackson Cacini, an Eastern Illinois commit, was 24 of 38 passing for 301 yards and four touchdowns with one interception. Matthew Donnelly ran 15 times for 111 yards and a touchdown and had five catches for 87 yards and two scores. entries.summary: <p>The road to the Class 8A state championship goes through Loyola and Mount Carmel. The teams have won the last four titles. So <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/high-school-football/scores/2026/10/15/high-school-football-scores-week-8" >Friday’s</a> regular-season finale between the state powerhouses had been circled on many calendars for months.</p><p>Over those months, the teams switched positions. The Caravan dropped from the top spot in the Super 25 and Loyola ascended to No. 1.</p><p>Friday in Wilmette, the dominant football team Mount Carmel saw itself as, and that many others envisioned back in August, started to become a reality.</p><p>The No. 4 Caravan dominated top-ranked Loyola much more than the 38-21 score indicates. Both teams pulled their starters with Mount Carmel leading by 24 in the final six minutes.</p><p>“There is a tendency to believe all the stuff they read,” Ramblers coach John Holecek said. “Now they understand we have to get better and we can’t make mistakes.”</p><p>The Ramblers (8-1, 2-1 CCL Blue) headed into the showdown against Mount Carmel (7-2, 2-1) averaging 36 points against a tough schedule. Both the passing and rushing games were putting up impressive yardage totals.</p><p>The Caravan held Loyola's starters to just 31 rushing yards.</p><p>“All week during practice, especially after we lost that [Brother Rice] game, we knew we had to step up,” Mount Carmel linebacker Roman Igwebuike said. “After practice, this is easy. We come after it every day. We came out tonight, and we knew we had to put it all on the line.”</p><p>Ramblers quarterback Matthew Lee was 13-for-24 for 177 yards with two touchdowns.</p><p>“Hopefully it goes another way if we have to play them again,” Holecek said. “[Mount Carmel] is a heck of a team. entries.title: Bulls guard Josh Giddey is preparing himself for the upcoming air show
entries.summary: <p>It’s not that the Adelaide 36ers didn’t have some talented hoopers on the roster when Josh Giddey was coming up in Australia’s National Basketball League.</p><p>But it’s called the “Land Down Under” for a reason, and that’s where most of the talent played when it came to the rim game.</p><p>There were some athletes in Oklahoma City when Giddey broke into the NBA. Some. But by the time he was traded to the Bulls, it was again a gravity-filled team for the most part – minus Zach LaVine for a few months before the 2025 trade deadline.</p><p>“I’ve just never played with those guys that are like high-flyers above the rim,” Giddey said, before smirking, “I played with Vooch (Nikola Vucevic) the last few years, and all due respect to Vooch, but he’s not an athletic, above-the-rim guy.”</p><p>My, how times have changed for Giddey.</p><p>Friday’s 133-116 preseason finale Bulls win was a reminder of that, and it came just a few minutes into the game against Minnesota when Caleb Wilson took two dribbles down the lane and erupted with a thunderous two-handed slam.</p><p>It’s not just Wilson in the arsenal, either. There’s Matas Buzelis on the other wing, Nic Claxton in the middle when he gets healthy, and even Leonard Miller and Noa Essengue off the bench. Giddey deems himself a player-maker, but even he knows he needs to get the lob game on point.</p><p>“I feel like I can throw pretty much every pass, and lobs are just one that I’ve never really had to throw a lot in my career,” Giddey said.</p><p>That’s about to change.</p><p>He’s been working on it in practice and throughout the preseason, but the nice thing is there’s room for error. Or in this case room for air. Buzelis and Wilson allow that just because of their vertical jump and catch radius.</p><p>“All these bigs I’ve played with have been really good in their own ways, but it’s been good to have a different look where that gives me the ability to put the ball near the rim and have guys go get it,” Giddey said. “Whether it’s wings or our fives, we’ve got guys that can catch lobs all around. I’ve got to get better at throwing them, but I think it’s going to be good to have guys that I can kind of put it anywhere around the cylinder and they’ll go take care of the rest.”</p><p>Not the only good Giddey sees with this group, either.</p><p>Besides having long, athletic wings, he has scoring potential around him. That’s why there will be so much focus on him this season.</p><p>It’s on Giddey, who finished with 12 points and four assists against the Timberwolves, to share the vision that coach Tiago Splitter has for this offense and execute it.</p><p>“I think he has a lot of guys that can score around him, so he knows that,” Splitter said of Giddey. “He’s thinking about the game, he’s smart about it, and hopefully game-by-game our vision starts to get a little more clear and he can help this team to be effective.”</p><p>Which is all the point guard wants. There are few players on the roster that are as self-aware as Giddey is. He knows social media outlets either praise him as a player or want him traded tomorrow.</p><p>That either or really seemed to be amplified this offseason, loud enough for Giddey to hear it. In his estimation it comes with the business.</p><p>“That’s social media for you,” Giddey said. “But I don’t ever try and allow stuff like that influence how I play. Everyone is entitled to their opinion, and whether they love me as a player, hate me, whatever it is, my job is the same every night, which is to try and make players around me better and that’s what I try to do.”</p>

entries.title: Sunday starts a crucial 5-day test for Bears coach Ben Johnson and his QB
entries.summary: <p>Sunday’s humiliation at Lambeau Field was the Bears’ worst loss since Week 2 last year, when Ben Johnson lost his Ford Field homecoming by 31 points.</p><p>The <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> responded by winning nine of their next 10 games.</p><p>If they’re going to rebound again this year, it has to start Sunday <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/10/16/bears-list-qb-caleb-williams-as-questionable-vs-falcons-but-full-week-of-practice-points-toward-return" target="_blank" >in Atlanta</a>, the first of two games in five days. How the Bears respond to the loss to their rivals will be a test of not only their quarterback — Caleb Williams is on track to start — but their head coach. Both were the catalysts of last year’s run, which turned an 0-2 team into a 9-3 ballclub — and the eventual NFC North champion.</p><p>Whether they can do it again is another question.</p><p>"That story has yet to be written,” Johnson said Friday. “We get a chance to do that ourselves. I feel strongly about our locker room. I think we have a lot of high-quality character guys … So far this week, they've handled it. It's all been back to business as usual. There's no moping around or ‘woe-is-me.’ They understand it's a long season, and everything's still out in front of us. We still have a winning record. That's a good thing and we have a lot to play for here going forward.”</p><p>As if the challenge of rebounding wasn’t difficult enough, the week leading into the Falcons game was rocky, with defensive end Montez Sweat being suspended two games for a performance-enhancing drug violation and Williams airing his grievances about the reporting about his injury. Johnson said Friday he “didn’t feel any frustration” from Williams, short of him trying to navigate his first major NFL absence.</p><p>The 3-2 Bears’ four-game stretch heading into their bye is filled with prime-time games and primo matchups. After Sunday’s game, they have a quick turnaround to face the defending AFC champion Patriots on “Thursday Night Football.” They then face the Super Bowl champion Seahawks on “Monday Night Football” and the Buccaneers on “Sunday Night Football” before taking a week off.</p><p>“This next stretch before the bye week, it's a big part,” Johnson said. “It's a big part of our story for this 2026 team.”</p><p>So is Williams, who is on track to make his first start since tearing his hamstring on a soggy Soldier Field turf against the Vikings. The Bears won two games in a row without him — one with Case Keenum and the other with Tyson Bagent — before Bagent looked lost in the Packers loss.</p><p>Williams took lessons from Keenum’s play in the “MNF” win against the Eagles.</p><p>“He was super decisive, super clean with getting the ball out,” Williams said. “The operation was really clean. Getting the ball in the guy's hands with a runner’s ball. … The night before the game, the QBs have a meeting, and Case was sharp as can be. In that meeting, it's just him being able to speak up and communicate. Then throughout the week the same, just Case being able to step up and communicate.”</p><p>Johnson doesn’t want Williams to try to be Keenum. Far from it. But being decisive with his throws and efficient with his movements will help protect the hamstring that Williams admitted isn’t fully healed.</p><p>“We’re trying to find that healthy balance between him being the player that he is that makes him so special — but also being smart and making sure we’re getting the ball to our playmakers in a timely fashion as well,” Johnson said. “So do I expect him to be a completely different player just because he sat down for a few weeks? No. When he comes back, he’s going to continue to learn. He’s going to continue to grow.”</p><p>Williams will be tested against his peers over the next week. Falcons quarterback Michael Penix was chosen seven spots after Williams in the 2024 draft. The choice shocked the Bears, who were thrilled that it allowed them to take receiver Rome Odunze with the next choice. Penix, who missed the end of the Falcons’ Sunday night overtime loss to the Ravens with a ribs injury, practiced all week and was declared healthy enough to start Sunday. </p><p>Thursday, the Bears will face off against Drake Maye, who missed winning the MVP last year by one first-place vote. He struggled in the Super Bowl and again to start the season before leading the Patriots to 74 points over the past two games.</p><p>Williams, of course, helped the Bears toward 59 points in the opener — and then three in Week 2 before his injury.</p><p>“He was on an upward trajectory before the injury happened,” Johnson said. “And I expect him to pick up where he left off and continue on that same path.”</p><p>Running back D’Andre Swift said he believes this year’s team has the same grit as last season’s squad. Now they have to prove it.</p><p>“You still have to put the work in, go out there and perform well enough to make that happen,” he said. “Ain’t nobody down or anything like that. We’re just ready for the next opportunity to try to get back on track.”</p>

entries.title: Rising mortgage rates and home prices sidelining buyers but now is the time to purchase, report says
entries.summary: <p>Hopeful buyers poured into open houses across the North Side over the summer. Some real estate agents reported nearly 100 people touring their listings.</p><p>But Keller Williams One Chicago Realtor Tommy Choi had less than 30 people recently visit his listing in Lincoln Park, one of the city’s hottest real estate markets. </p><p>There were four offers on the townhome, though a few months ago he would’ve expected about 10. While the property sold for nearly $100,000 over its asking price, it would've likely commanded much higher in the summer — when the market was more competitive and prompted <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2026/08/01/cash-properties-sale-open-house-chicago-homebuyers-bidding-wars" target="_blank" >bidding wars</a> across Chicago.</p><p>The housing market slows down in the fall, as children return to school and families prep for the upcoming holiday season. But it also means buyers — who've struggled for months to find a home in their budget — could score a discount.</p><p>A Redfin report found October is the best time for homebuyers to score a deal in Chicago, as well as 15 other major cities such as Boston, Philadelphia and Orlando. "The seasonal sweet spot represents the time when discounts off a home’s original asking price — through price cuts or negotiations — are typically near their highest," according to the September report.</p><p>“The sellers that are still struggling to get offers come October are going to be more willing to accept an offer below listing price or to lower the price themselves — or offer other sweeteners,” Redfin Chief Economist Daryl Fairweather said. “It's really because they want to get things done. They don't want to have this home sale hanging over their heads going into the holidays. As a buyer, that means that you're going to be having sellers that are more willing to negotiate with you than they would have been in summer or spring.”</p><p>October has historically offered better opportunities for homebuyers, data from Illinois Realtors shows. Between 2021 and 2025, Chicago's median sale price in October was lower compared to June, typically the peak buying month, averaging a 10% decline. The trade association found a similar trend with a home's days on market — the longer a home sits, the more willing sellers are to accept price cuts or toss in other conditions to close a sale.</p><p>Ezekiel Morris, managing broker of EXIT Strategy Realty/EMA Management, said affordability and a lack of inventory have been the defining themes of Chicago’s housing market this year. He primarily serves the South Side and has seen some buyers broaden their search from North Side neighborhoods to the south.</p><p>He sees more opportunities this fall for buyers, especially those who qualify for down payment assistance and similar programs that can boost their budget.</p><p>“There's deals at every level,” Morris said.</p><p>While October can be a period of relief for buyers, prices have been rising — even in October. And mortgage rates have also climbed.</p><p>Redfin data shows in October 2020, the median sale price for a home in the Chicago metro area was $275,000. That figure soared by about 33% to $366,500 in October 2025. When compared to the market's peak time, data shows the median sale price in June 2020 was $269,000 and jumped to $407,000 in June 2025 — a roughly 51% increase.</p><div class="Enhancement" data-align-center> <div class="HtmlModule"><a class="AnchorLink" id="html-embed-module-800000" name="html-embed-module-800000"></a><div style="min-height:451px" id="datawrapper-vis-iHVaS"><script type="text/javascript" defer src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/iHVaS/embed.js" charset="utf-8" data-target="#datawrapper-vis-iHVaS"></script><noscript><img src="https://datawrapper.dwcdn.net/iHVaS/full.png" alt="Median Sale Price for a home in the Chicago Metro area in October, by year (Line chart)" /></noscript></div> </div> </div><p>Fairweather said nationally, a record number of buyers have backed out of purchasing homes, and pending home sales have plunged as rising mortgage rates cause people to change their mind. </p><p>September saw pending home sales in the U.S. drop 4% from August and 8.6% year over year. It's also the first time in three years that pending home sales declined in all 50 of the most populous U.S. metro markets. Chicago declined 5.8% year over year and the share of deals under contract that fell through was 14.1%, Redfin said. </p><p>Tracking pending home sales can give real-time insight into the housing market and quickly reflect the impact of rising mortgage rates on consumers. </p><p>The average rate on a 30-year fixed-rate mortgage was 7.40%, the same as last week, Freddie Mac said Thursday. One year ago, the average rate was 6.27%.</p><p>“Chicago is kind of different from the national market because there aren't enough sellers … and there are more buyers in Chicago compared to other parts of the country,” Fairweather said. “But even so, October is the best time to negotiate because those sellers that haven't sold yet are going to be willing to lower their price. But the high mortgage rates have just priced out a lot of people who just can't work it under these higher mortgage rates. So if you're still in the market right now, then you really aren't facing much buyer competition at all — and the sellers are willing to work with you.”</p><p>Dan Gjeldum, executive vice president of mortgage lending at CrossCountry Mortgage, thinks <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/real-estate/2024/09/27/federal-reserve-interest-rate-cuts-homeowners-boost-refinance-mortgage-buy" >interest rates </a>have been increasing faster than normal this year. He said it’s partly due to the war in Iran, which is impacting everything from inflation to oil prices.</p><p>“Inflation's the arch enemy of mortgage rates, or interest rates in general,” he said.</p><p>Mortgage rate increases have reset the expectations of many buyers, Gjeldum said. CrossCountry has also seen fewer prospective clients than usual, and Gjeldum has been reaching out to pre-approved clients to discuss how the rate changes may impact their monthly mortgage payment.</p><p>“It gets quieter as we move into [the end of the year]. But with the interest rate changes, some people have definitely paused,” he said. “I think once people accept rates are up and they get comfortable with that, then it will pick right back up. Our timing right now is definitely a lull.”</p><p>But experts and real estate agents said it’s still possible to get a good deal. That’s because even with higher mortgage rates, it may still be a better value to buy in the fall as prices are higher during the spring and summer buying season, Choi said. It's also hard to predict if, and by how much, rates will fall next year.</p><p>“That's the conversation that I'm having with buyers that are serious and active right now, and those are the buyers that are going to win,” Choi said.</p><p>Gjeldum said the end of the year can be full of opportunities — it’s always when he’s bought new property — but it depends on a buyer's financial situation.</p><p>“Talk to your mortgage professional, get an idea of what your payments are going to be and if you have to adjust your budget, you have to adjust your budget," he said.</p>

entries.title: Thrifting is for need, not for greed
entries.summary: <p>I grew up as the youngest of nine children in a household where my parents worked modest jobs, stretching every dollar to keep us fed, clothed and sheltered. One of my mother’s greatest resources was the thrift store.</p><p>I remember those shopping trips vividly. When the doors opened, she instructed us to grab armfuls of clothing and bring them to her. With a discerning eye, she sorted through someone else’s donations, matching sizes and styles to her children. Somehow, she made it work.</p><p>Those trips were about more than clothing. They were about dignity. Thrift stores allowed families like ours to look and feel good without sacrificing money needed for food, utilities or rent. They provided affordability without shame.</p><p>Fast-forward to today, and something has changed.</p><p>Thrifting has become trendy. Resellers, influencers and celebrities have helped transform secondhand shopping into a profitable enterprise. What was once a lifeline for families with limited resources has increasingly become a marketplace where popularity drives prices and profit overshadows purpose.</p><p>The irony? Items donated freely are sometimes priced comparably to merchandise in retail stores.</p><p>When did donated clothing become a luxury? When did affordability become exclusivity? And when did the people who relied on these stores become an afterthought?</p><p>There is nothing wrong with embracing sustainable fashion or finding hidden treasures. But there is something troubling about an industry that benefits from generosity while pricing out people who depend on it.</p><p>Working with underserved communities, I see how rising costs force families to make difficult choices. Affordable clothing should not become another financial burden.</p><p>Thrift stores must reconsider their priorities. Donations should represent an opportunity to provide access, not simply maximize revenue.</p><p>My mother didn’t take us thrifting to make a fashion statement. She took us because nine children needed clothes, and she was determined to provide them without compromising our dignity.</p><p>Somewhere along the way, we turned necessity into novelty and affordability into excess.</p><p>The greatest value of a donated item isn’t how much someone will pay for it, but what it means to someone who otherwise couldn’t afford it.</p><p>Dignity should never become a luxury.</p><p><i>Kim Jay, training manager and senior community health worker,</i><b><i> </i></b><i>Sinai Urban Health Institute</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-910000" name="module-910000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h3>Give us your take</h3><br>Send letters to the editor to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. To be considered for publication, letters must include your full name, your neighborhood or hometown and a phone number for verification purposes. Letters should be a maximum of approximately 375 words.</div> </div><p></p><h3>Study: Most Americans OK with athletes talking politics as long as they’re white</h3><p>Indiana Fever guard Sophie Cunningham recently gained national attention after declaring her <a class="Link" href="https://www.espn.com/wnba/story/_/id/49306657/sophie-cunningham-finger-point-indiana-fever-wnba" target="_blank" >opposition</a> to the participation of transgender athletes in women’s sports. These comments were <a class="Link" href="https://www.mediamatters.org/fox-news/fox-news-has-spent-over-13-12-hours-waging-wnba-culture-war-summer" target="_blank" >embraced</a> by Fox News and denounced by the <a class="Link" href="https://www.nytimes.com/athletic/7499786/2026/08/07/wnba-union-transgender-sophie-cunningham/" target="_blank" >WNBA’s Players Association</a>. Soon after, Cunningham had a run-in with Chicago Sky guard DiJonai Carrington, who after being ejected for a foul on Cunningham, wrote the words “WHITE PRIVILEGE” on Instagram. Carrington was criticized by many of the <a class="Link" href="https://www.youtube.com/watch?v=1H-6hwKU4dw" target="_blank" >same conservative pundits</a> who lauded Cunningham, even as Carrington's words were celebrated by <a class="Link" href="https://sports.yahoo.com/articles/jemele-hill-comes-defense-dijonai-133900308.html" target="_blank" >progressives</a> who attacked Cunningham.</p><p>The polarized reactions to Cunningham and Carrington raise the question of whether the race of the speaker affects public support for athletes’ political speech. We used this controversy to find out.</p><p>In August, we fielded an experiment on a <a class="Link" href="https://www.umass.edu/poll/" target="_blank" >nationally representative survey</a>. We randomly assigned respondents to one of three groups and asked them how acceptable it is for professional athletes to speak publicly about political issues. In the control condition, we asked the question without referencing any specific player. Respondents in the other two experimental conditions were asked the same question, but with the mention of Carrington or Cunningham, who have racially distinctive <a class="Link" href="https://www.jstor.org/stable/pdf/26563296.pdf?casa_token=DZCK5SdmspwAAAAA:9Ujny3C3K2xemseWvBxhYdQlACFIzy-uxs9DzWZlkleotZzLMwWkcY0nydXGgmpxhBGvYvGRV45ohU0jRgV3yygoE_zClsg140RF4weHZ0BvgpbCS29_" target="_blank" >names</a>. This allowed us to test whether identifying a specific player changed Americans’ views about athletes making political statements, as decades of <a class="Link" href="https://www.annualreviews.org/content/journals/10.1146/annurev.soc.33.040406.131740" target="_blank" >research on racial discrimination</a> have revealed Americans can recognize the race of individuals from their names.</p><p>Our experiment shows that Americans are more likely to approve of athletes who voice their political views when those athletes are white (as opposed to Black). Sixty-nine percent of those asked about Cunningham approved of athletes speaking publicly, while only 57% of those asked about Carrington approved.</p><p>We then examined the differences in attitudes among the most <a class="Link" href="https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/ps-political-science-and-politics/article/fear-institutionalized-racism-and-empathy-the-underlying-dimensions-of-whites-racial-attitudes/F6205AFDA74F11AAAA518DA240AC7995" target="_blank" >racially prejudiced</a> Americans, and found that these individuals were much more likely to support athletes’ political speech when a white athlete was mentioned. While 62% of the most racially prejudiced in the Carrington group opposed professional athletes making political statements, among the most racially prejudiced respondents in the Cunningham group, 64% supported professional athletes making political statements, with only 36% in opposition.</p><p>As the WNBA continues to grow, debates over what its players can say will likely intensify. Our findings suggest that these debates are not simply about whether athletes should speak out. They are also about who is speaking.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://nam10.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fpolsci.umass.edu%2Fpeople%2Ftatishe-m-nteta&data=05%7C02%7Cnteta%40polsci.umass.edu%7C9d694a2587ca4c9aedbe08df1b1d9aae%7C7bd08b0b33954dc194bbd0b2e56a497f%7C0%7C0%7C639259486164363182%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=XDugLWvuaWEkGPUehXNjD%2ByPDH3yWNXCSETewvy1DH0%3D&reserved=0" target="_blank" ><i>Tatishe Nteta</i></a><i>, provost professor of political science, University of Massachusetts at Amherst and director, UMass Poll</i></p><p><a class="Link" href="https://nam10.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fwww.umass.edu%2Fpolitical-science%2Fabout%2Fdirectory%2Fjesse-rhodes&data=05%7C02%7Cnteta%40polsci.umass.edu%7C9d694a2587ca4c9aedbe08df1b1d9aae%7C7bd08b0b33954dc194bbd0b2e56a497f%7C0%7C0%7C639259486164378595%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=C5DBy%2FmdPKfKck4NTFDC5S6nc4KtIT1zm5woDBA2yCM%3D&reserved=0" target="_blank" ><i>Jesse Rhodes</i></a><i>, professor of political science, University of Massachusetts at Amherst and co-director, UMass Poll</i></p><p><a class="Link" href="https://nam10.safelinks.protection.outlook.com/?url=https%3A%2F%2Fpolsci.umass.edu%2Fpeople%2Fadam-eichen&data=05%7C02%7Cnteta%40polsci.umass.edu%7C9d694a2587ca4c9aedbe08df1b1d9aae%7C7bd08b0b33954dc194bbd0b2e56a497f%7C0%7C0%7C639259486164393484%7CUnknown%7CTWFpbGZsb3d8eyJFbXB0eU1hcGkiOnRydWUsIlYiOiIwLjAuMDAwMCIsIlAiOiJXaW4zMiIsIkFOIjoiTWFpbCIsIldUIjoyfQ%3D%3D%7C0%7C%7C%7C&sdata=dUt4SR69ZIqyakWcBZBh%2BaYwjyDhbzYRV0v6wUFoGYE%3D&reserved=0" target="_blank" ><i>Adam Eichen</i></a><i>, doctoral student in political science, University of Massachusetts at Amherst and graduate research fellow, UMass Poll</i></p><h3>Death penalty disagreement</h3><p>Reader Michael Hart recently <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/letters-to-the-editor/2026/10/07/death-penalty-christa-pike-avalon-regal-theater-ohare-express-trump-schmitt-sox-bears" >wrote</a> about his stance against the death penalty. I beg to differ.</p><p>Mr. Hart wrote: “There were certainly some (executions ) carried out in error.” Perhaps this was true a century ago, but since capital punishment was reinstated by the Supreme Court in 1976, I ask him to produce definitive evidence or proof of any wrongful executions. </p><p>Some years ago in Illinois, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/politics/2021/7/8/22568299/anthony-porter-illinois-death-penalty-dies" >Anthony Porter</a> was freed from death row (and from prison) after it was ascertained he was wrongly convicted in a double fatal shooting. This case was held up as an example showing the death penalty was broken. Porter was indeed exonerated. But Alstory Simon, who confessed to the murder, was released from prison after he said he was coerced to make a statement by a private investigator working with the journalism students .</p><p>The Death Penalty Information Center that Mr. Hart cites would like the public to believe it is an unbiased group. In reality, it is an anti-death penalty organization with an agenda.</p><p>If Mr. Hart is concerned about the time between sentencing and execution, saying this is “cruel and unusual punishment “ and “torture," I can see his point. It’s cruel and torturous to the families of the murder victims. I’m definitely in favor of speeding up this time frame.</p><p>When I was 11 years old, my oldest brother, Frank, was murdered during a holdup. He was 25 years old. You want to know about torture and cruel and unusual punishment? Try living with that for the rest of your life. Try watching your parents mourn and grieve every day. And try watching his killers spend less than 10 years in prison.</p><p><i>David G. Foys, Westmont</i></p><h3>Obama is still on the hook for labor promises </h3><p>The contradiction between the values Barack Obama championed and the working conditions employees should be able to expect at the Obama Foundation and Obama Presidential Center must be glaring.</p><p>That’s exactly what makes this situation so troubling. Obama built much of his political message around standing up for working people, supporting organized labor, protecting workers rights and making sure people received fair wages and benefits. He even said, <a class="Link" href="https://obamawhitehouse.archives.gov/the-press-office/remarks-president-obama-afl-cio-executive-council" target="_blank" >“labor unions are a big part of the solution.”</a></p><p>So how is it that institutions bearing his name have employees who feel the need to <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/news/2026/10/07/obama-foundation-and-center-workers-unionize-open-letter-afscme" >organize a union</a> to secure the pay, benefits and working conditions they believe they deserve?</p><p>The question isn’t whether the employees have to form a union. The question is why employees feel they need a union to have a meaningful voice in the first place.</p><p>A union should never be viewed as a failure of the workplace. But when the person whose legacy inspired an institution championed workers rights and collective bargaining, it is fair to ask whether those principles are being reflected in the treatment of the people who work there.</p><p>The true test of a commitment to working people isn’t what you say when you’re running for office. It’s how you treat the people working for you when you no longer need their votes.</p><p><i>Timothy “Tim” Thomas Jr., Auburn Gresham</i></p><h3>Flocking over college students</h3><p>Elgin Community College’s trash bag standoff with Flock Safety, described in WBEZ's Lisa Kurian Philip's recent <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/education/2026/10/09/to-protect-immigrant-students-a-chicago-area-college-told-flock-to-remove-its-cameras-the-company-refused" >story</a> — “To protect immigrant students, a Chicago-area college told Flock to remove its cameras. The company refused" — is less a privacy dispute than a lesson in who owns a campus.</p><p>In April 2025 the college rented six surveillance cameras. When U.S. Immigration and Customs Enforcement detained a student in a campus lot and enrollment slipped, President Peggy Heinrich asked that the cameras come down. Flock refused, then ignored an offer to pay out the remaining months. Staff covered the lenses with bags and zip ties. Unmarked workers stripped the bags off. The cameras stayed until the contract expired in April.</p><p>That is the tell. A public college could not shut off equipment on its own property because the vendor kept title. Safety had been leased, and the lease ran one way.</p><p>Records show immigration authorities searched Flock data from other Illinois campuses, including Joliet Junior College and both University of Illinois campuses. Although Elgin Community College own audit found no such search, caution was the right call. More than half of its students are Hispanic, and a camera that logs plates, dents and bumper stickers does not distinguish a stolen car from a student driving to class.</p><p>Illinois colleges still running these readers should ask one question before renewing: If the board votes tomorrow to pull the plug, can it? If the answer is no, the campus is not securing its students. It is renting them out.</p><p><i>Ronald Beaty, West Barnstable, Massachusetts</i></p><h3>Americans worth honoring</h3><p>In her recent <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/other-views/2026/10/07/christopher-columbus-italian-american-pride-indigenous-native-chicago-selena-fragassi" >op-ed</a> on Christopher Columbus, Selena Fragassi wrote, “I’d be the first to stand on the hill of needing strong examples of Italian pride in this country.”</p><p>I would like to add <a class="Link" href="https://www.money.org/frank-gasparro-u-s-mints-former-chief-engraver-dies/" target="_blank" >Frank Gasparro</a>, the 10th chief engraver of the U.S. Mint, to her list. </p><p>Gasparro designed the reverse side of the <a class="Link" href="https://stacksbowers.com/coin-resource-center/half-dollars/kennedy-half-dollar/kennedy-half-dollar-type-1-90-silver/" target="_blank" >Kennedy half dollar</a>. For the U.S. Bicentennial, he designed the <a class="Link" href="https://www.usmint.gov/content/usmint/us/en/learn/coins-and-medals/bicentennial-coins-and-medals.html?srsltid=AU7gw4U1Q6-_-YuE22WwLr3sq_fgMnRFvyysQBL5Vb7Wa3KmsdajsRbO" target="_blank" >National Medal</a>. He created the <a class="Link" href="https://coinweek.com/john-wayne-congressional-gold-medal-collectors-guide/" target="_blank" >medal that Congress awarded</a> John Wayne. And in Gasparro's most widely known accomplishment, he designed the reverse side of the <a class="Link" href="https://www.littletoncoin.com/shop/lincoln-memorial-cents" target="_blank" >Lincoln Memorial penny</a> </p><p>Also, I agree with Fragassi that we should have a special day “to honor those who are our true American pioneers.”</p><p>Indigenous peoples have been here for <a class="Link" href="https://aeon.co/essays/the-first-americans-a-story-of-wonderful-uncertain-science" target="_blank" >thousands of years</a>. In that time, they discovered and sampled every plant growing in the Americas. Thanks to them we have the <a class="Link" href="https://www.bloomsbury.com/uk/columbian-exchange-9780275980733/" target="_blank" >four great gifts</a> of corn, potatoes, tomatoes and cocoa beans. So next year and in years yet to come, let Chicago be in the forefront of celebrating a more inclusive holiday by calling it (the day we traditionally know as Columbus Day) Explorers Day. That way we can all join together in honoring the accomplishments of many people.</p><p><i>William Dodd Brown, Lincoln Square </i></p><h3>Faithful friends</h3><p>Excellent <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/13/university-of-chicago-sexual-assault-alpha-epsilon-pi" >reporting </a>on the sexual assault at the University of Chicago campus, Sophie Sherry, Rosemary Sobol and Mary Norkol. The two women who saved their friend are sheroes! Thank you for the well-written article. I’m sure this was painful to cover, but I love the brave silver lining of women’s friendship.</p><p><i>Laura Brancky, Glenview</i></p><h3>High costs</h3><p>Is it my imagination, or are all consumer goods manufacturers raising prices? I just spent $9 for a small bag of Gardetto’s and a diet Coke. Thanks, Donald Trump.</p><p> <i>John Hankes , Streeterville </i></p><h3>Price isn’t right</h3><p>President Donald Trump is trying to make a deal with voters by promising to pay adult Americans <a class="Link" href="https://www.npr.org/2026/09/09/nx-s1-5961045/republican-midterm-convention-dallas-trump-vance" target="_blank" >$5,000</a> if the Republican Party maintains control of Congress. Any voter thinking about accepting Trump‘s offer to pay off voters should consider how to artfully take advantage of the deal. Hold out for a least <a class="Link" href="https://www.washingtonpost.com/politics/porn-star-was-paid-130000-to-keep-quiet-about-a-relationship-with-trump-wall-street-journal-reports/2018/01/12/fde75e72-f7ef-11e7-91af-31ac729add94_story.html" target="_blank" >$130,000</a>, the reported amount Trump paid Stormy Daniels to stay quiet about their alleged sexual encounter.</p><p><i>Alan Rhine, Glenview</i></p>
