entries.title: Hate comes for South Asians — again
entries.summary: <p>I'll never forget the burning sensation prickling across my face as I overheard condescending laughter when my mother, an Indian immigrant, first volunteered at my elementary school cafeteria.</p><p>I didn't push back against my classmates' snide commentary on her nose ring — a style of adornment believed to have been <a class="Link" href="https://timesofindia.indiatimes.com/life-style/fashion/buzz/timeless-allure-of-the-indian-nose-ring-the-nath-a-glimpse-into-its-history-significance-and-styles/photostory/104559716.cms?picid=104559742" target="_blank" >introduced by the Mughals</a> when they arrived in India in the 16th century.</p><p>Instead, I directed my anger and humiliation toward my poor mother, demanding she take the colorless stud out of her nose the next time she showed up at school.</p><p>I learned to perfect the art of flinching internally at every anti-Indian slur and bigoted, tone-deaf remark lobbed my way when I came of age in the 1980s in a mostly white north suburb that bordered the city.</p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-floatRight><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-380000" name="module-380000"></a> <div class="RichTextSidebarModule-title">Columnist </div> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody"><h2>Columnists</h2></div> </div><p>"No offense," a so-called junior high school friend once prefaced before claiming the presence of Indians at a Marshall Field's was a definitive sign the iconic department store chain's prestige was plummeting.</p><p>Another time, a teacher pulled me aside and suggested my mom give a classroom presentation on why she wears a red dot on her forehead.</p><p>My mother used to create makeshift bindis above her eyes with lipstick and kajal as a fashion statement when she first arrived in the United States. But as a Muslim woman, she'd hardly be an expert on <a class="Link" href="https://www.britannica.com/topic/bindi" target="_blank" >bindis </a>and other forehead markings' spiritual significance in Hinduism, Buddhism and Jainism.</p><p>Watching the rise of immigrants and U.S.-born Americans of South Asian descent, many of my Gen X friends and I find ourselves fantasizing about what it would have been like, as teenagers, to watch someone like Zohran Mamdani, who was born in Uganda, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/columnists/2025/06/14/new-york-city-mayoral-elections-zohran-mamdani-muslim-indian-gaza-palestinians-cuomo-rummana-column" target="_blank" ><u>run New York City</u></a> or see model Bhavitha Mandava, a native of Hyderabad, open a <a class="Link" href="https://www.vogue.com/article/bhavitha-mandava-chanel-metiers-dart-2025" target="_blank" ><u>Chanel runway show</u></a>.</p><p>Unfortunately, the same visibility we cheer on, coupled with xenophobic narratives about H-1B visas and "job-stealing foreigners," has unleashed a tidal wave of anti-South Asian hate, which <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/crime/2026/10/15/gun-jammed-when-neo-nazi-tried-to-commit-mass-shooting-at-hindu-temple-in-aurora-prosecutors-say" >allegedly motivated</a> an attempted mass shooting at a Hindu temple in Aurora last weekend.</p><p>Online vitriol against South Asians — Indians, Pakistanis, Bangladeshis and others — proliferated by 240% between January 2024 and June 2026, according to a <a class="Link" href="https://www.csohate.org/press-releases/anti-south-asian-hate-united-states-2026/" target="_blank" >recent report</a> by the Center for the Study of Organized Hate.</p><p>Just a month ago, Bo French, an anti-Muslim and anti-immigrant Republican running for a seat on the Texas Railroad Commission, spewed such hate when he <a class="Link" href="https://x.com/bofrench/status/2099118916282810552?s=20" target="_blank" >shared a photo </a>on X of South Asian University of Texas at Austin students celebrating a football victory.</p><p>"I heard UT graduation this year looked like this. I didn’t believe it. The problem is now obviously far worse than anyone imagined," wrote French, who has promoted the racist "Great Replacement" conspiracy theory. </p><p>Hate targeting South Asians never disappeared. The ugliness has only been repackaged, and like previous smear campaigns, it doesn't spare the most prominent members of our communities.</p><p>"We must come together to confront the hatred that put so many innocent lives at risk," <a class="Link" href="https://x.com/CongressmanRaja/status/2110730618581520749" target="_blank" >said</a> U.S. Rep. Raja Krishnamoorthi, D-Ill., who was at the west suburban Sri Venkateswara Swami (Balaji) Temple when the alleged gunman's AR-style rifle jammed, foiling the deadly plot.</p><p>I agree. Speaking up is key. If Alexandros Paporakis' co-workers at an Arlington Heights Taco Bell hadn't alerted authorities, the 19-year-old neo-Nazi might have tried again to carry out his alleged plan and succeeded. </p><p>More Americans need to similarly raise their voices, including the South Asians who are in proximity to the poison.</p><p>Too often these desis wilt before bigots and are willing to throw other marginalized communities under the bus, including South Asians who don't share the same motherland, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/opinion/2021/3/17/22335258/chicago-city-council-resolution-denouncing-bigotry-discrimination-india-bjp-modi" >religion</a> or <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/columnists/2024/05/17/caste-system-india-yashica-dutt-dalit-ambedkar-gandhi-muslims-black-america-rummana-hussain" >caste</a>.</p><p>Less than 10 years after Donald Trump <a class="Link" href="https://www.politico.com/story/2016/10/donald-trump-bollywood-india-hindus-new-jersey-229848" target="_blank" >blurted</a> "I’m a big fan of Hindu," his foe turned second-in-command, JD Vance, defended a government employee who had made a social media plea to <a class="Link" href="https://www.pbs.org/newshour/politics/vance-says-doge-staffer-who-resigned-after-a-report-of-racist-postings-should-be-brought-back" target="_blank" >“normalize Indian hate</a>."</p><p>Vance's wife, <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/columnists/2024/07/19/jd-vance-usha-chilukuri-indian-interracial-marriage-racism-trump-white-supremacy-rummana-hussain" >Usha Vance</a>, the daughter of Indian immigrants and a Hindu, called the post <a class="Link" href="https://www.yahoo.com/news/usha-vance-asked-jd-calling-170431262.html" target="_blank" >“terrible”</a> but hasn't publicly said much about her husband's stance on the matter or his other positions that can potentially harm South Asian communities.</p><h3>Apathy isn’t an option </h3><p>I was only a child when I was unable to muster the courage to respond to my juvenile tormentors.</p><p><a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/columnists/2023/5/19/23728390/vivek-ramaswamy-republican-candidate-president-south-shore-migrants-town-hall-rummana-hussain-column" >Vivek Ramaswamy</a> was 40 when he meekly countered white Christians half his age who <a class="Link" href="https://newrepublic.com/post/201664/vivek-ramaswamy-turning-point-racism-ohio" target="_blank" >questioned</a> how he — a Hindu — could serve as Ohio governor at a Turning Point USA event in 2025.</p><p>My siblings and I wish we could go back in time and tell our younger selves that many of our bullies would eventually go on to embrace many aspects of our culture.</p><p>For example, a boy who pestered my brother over our mother's nose piercing, ended up dating a man with a nose ring.</p><p>Karma is a boomerang, as they say. </p><p>I have since apologized to my mom for my no-nose ring request. </p><p>My mom said she didn't mind.</p><p>But I do remember she forgot to ice my skin when she gleefully pierced my nose with a heated needle when I was in college.</p><p>Perhaps it was payback. Or maybe it was an on-the-nose reminder to never remain numb.</p><p><i>Rummana Hussain is a columnist and leads the opinion coverage at the Sun-Times.</i></p><div class="RichTextSidebarModule Enhancement" data-module data-align-center><a class="AnchorLink" id="module-2d0000" name="module-2d0000"></a> <div class="RichTextModule-items RichTextBody">Send letters to <a class="Link" href="mailto:letters@suntimes.com" target="_blank" >letters@suntimes.com</a>. More about <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/submitting-opinion-and-letters" >how to submit here</a>.</div> </div><p></p>

entries.title: Dear Abby: Daughter with grudges makes herself hard to love
entries.summary: <p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> I have three grown children and seven grandchildren. I have solid relationships with my oldest and youngest, their spouses and their children. My middle daughter, "Hope," has always been distant. I've tried for years to build a relationship with her and her children.</p><p>Hope has suffered from mental and physical illness most of her life, and I'd like to be able to help her. The problem is that she keeps a house full of animals, and the place is unwelcoming to say the least. I've also tried keeping in touch via phone calls, but they always end up with her being critical and accusing me of things that happened a long time ago — some of which I wasn't even aware of. She has no relationships outside of her two children and no contact with her siblings.</p><p>I love Hope and her children, but I'm tired of the abuse. I have quit pushing myself on her, but I miss her so much. Is there any hope for us? — <i>LOSING HOPE IN ALABAMA</i></p><p><b>DEAR LOSING HOPE:</b> You don't want the door to close forever, so it's important to keep the lines of communication open. You can continue to call Hope and visit occasionally without enduring the abuse.</p><p>Each time she tries to steer the conversation in a negative direction, use the opportunity to introduce the idea of family counseling. Frame it as your desire to understand the past events she is still unhappy about. If you can get Hope to attend a few sessions with you, it may be a big step forward.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> A dear friend is obsessed with death and the grieving process. While her fixation is not entirely unusual, her actions are. She attends area funeral services two to four times a week for people she does not know. She sits in the back, rarely talks to family and friends, and leaves quietly, so she says it isn't a big deal. I disagree. I feel it's disrespectful to attend the funeral services of a stranger even if you are unobtrusive. What do you think? Am I wrong? — <i>PERPLEXED IN ARKANSAS</i></p><p><b>DEAR PERPLEXED:</b> It's hard to label a behavior disrespectful when it's causing no harm or distress to anyone. I don't know how isolated this friend of yours is, but this may be her way to be in the presence of others and cope with loneliness. Another reason could be that she enjoys hearing about people's lives. Rather than criticize or judge her, I think you should simply ask her why she does it. Her answer may be enlightening.</p><p><b>DEAR ABBY:</b> How can I get my nice, college-educated son-in-law to wipe his mouth with a napkin during meals instead of using his sleeve? — <i>FATHER-IN-LAW WITH MANNERS</i></p><p><b>DEAR F-I-L:</b> There are two ways to get the message across. The first would be to "remind" him in plain English while you are at the table. The second would be to speak to your daughter about it and ask her to get the message across.</p><p><i>Dear Abby is written by Abigail Van Buren. For nearly four decades, Jeanne Phillips penned this column, which was founded in 1956 by her mother, Pauline Phillips. Contact Dear Abby at www.DearAbby.com or P.O. Box 270135, Kansas City, MO 64127.</i></p>

entries.title: Bears-Falcons: What To Watch For
entries.summary: <p>Breaking down what to expect Sunday when the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears" target="_blank" >Bears</a> visit the <a class="Link" href="https://chicago.suntimes.com/bears/2026/10/15/bears-falcons-deep-ball-jaylon-johnson-dennis-allen-sunday-packers-jordan-love-nfl" target="_blank" >Falcons</a>:</p><h3><b>WHEN THE BEARS HAVE THE BALL</b></h3><p>Even after their clunker last week at Lambeau Field, the Bears’ rushing offense remains the best in the NFL. Their average of 173.2 yards is about 6 ½ yards more than the NFL’s second-ranked running team — Sunday’s opponent, the Falcons.</p><p>Bears coach Ben Johnson struggled to establish any offensive rhythm against the Packers. While it’s easy to blame the jumpy Tyson Bagent for their pass-game struggles, Johnson’s run scheme wasn’t much better. With Kyle Monangai out, he couldn’t find production from anyone other than starter D’Andre Swift, who ran nine times for a modest 43 yards.</p><p>The rest of the Bears ran 15 times for 38 yards. Roschon Johnson, who served as Swift’s backup, ran five times for six yards. Receiver Luther Burden had a seven-yard run — and three that lost a total of five yards.</p><p>The Bears’ 81 rushing yards were the third-fewest of the Johnson era. A week earlier, against the Jets, they'd run for the second-most. </p><p>Johnson needs to find a way to unlock the team’s run game with Swift on and off the field. The Falcons won’t provide much help — they’ve given up 80.2 rushing yards per game, the fourth-fewest in the NFL. Defensive tackles LaCale London and Gervon Dexter, who are both former Bears, rank in the top 16 of Pro Football Focus’ run defense grades at their position.</p><p>Sunday will be a test for Johnson, but also the Bears’ ballyhooed offensive line, which struggled against the Packers after spending all week trying to recover from playing 89 snaps against the Jets.</p><h3><b>WHEN THE FALCONS HAVE THE BALL</b></h3><p>One of the most alarming aspects of Montez Sweat’s suspension — and there were many — was how important his position is to trying to slow down all-world running back Bijan Robinson.</p><p>The Falcons run an outside zone rushing scheme in which they want to get defensive linemen to “run sideways,” defensive line coach Jeremy Garrett said, so Robinson can hunt for holes. The best want to slow the scheme is to push blockers back to create traffic before Robinson can get outside. The Bears figure to struggle to do that without Sweat, who will be out for two games, and Dayo Odeyingbo, who will sit out Sunday's game with an injured quad. The Bears will lean on reinforcements: Shemar Turner, the former second-round pick who returned this week from an ACL injury, and Jayden Loving and Jamree Kromah, who have never played in a regular-season game.</p><p>The Falcons’ offense is about more than an MVP-caliber running back, though. Receiver Drake London is fourth in the NFL with 488 receiving yards. He’s not a speedster but plays with tremendous physicality at the top of his routes.</p><p>Tight end Kyle Pitts has only 10 catches for 109 receiving yards this season but is a year removed from catching 88 balls for 928 yards.</p><p>Robinson leads the NFL with 580 rushing yards. His short-yardage backup, Brian Robinson, is ranked 31<sup>st</sup> in the NFL with 210. The two have four rushing touchdowns apiece.</p>

entries.title: Handful of competitive suburban races rev up November General Assembly elections
entries.summary: <p>A pair of suburban races for Springfield lawmakers are competitive fights heading into the Nov. 3 election, even as many incumbent politicians across the state are running unopposed.</p><p>Among the races to watch, Rep. Nabeela Syed, a Democrat from Inverness, is challenging incumbent Republican Darby Hills of Barrington Hills, who was appointed to the 26th District state Senate seat in early 2025. The northwest suburban district includes parts of Cook, Lake, McHenry and Kane counties.</p><p>Syed is completing her second term in the Illinois House after graduating from the University of California Berkeley in 2021, while Hills is completing the term of Dan McConchie, who resigned to take a job with a nonprofit organization.</p><p>The Illinois Democratic Party is spending heavily to help Syed with her campaign. In September alone, the party and a committee led by Illinois Senate President Don Harmon — with the aim of bolstering Democrats' majority — contributed almost $1 million to Syed, records show. </p><p>Affordability and access to health care are among her top priorities, says the Palatine native. “Knocking on doors, I see that pain and I see that struggle,” Syed says.</p><p>Hills, a former prosecutor and 2021 Mrs. Illinois America, was a Barrington Hills trustee before being appointed to McConchie’s seat. She has campaigned for public safety, especially related to children, lower taxes and controls on spending. </p><p>“Illinois doesn’t have a revenue problem,” Hills says, “it has a spending problem.”</p><p>Republican Party political committees contributed more than $80,000 to Hills in September after giving her more than $300,000 in August, according to state campaign disclosure reports.</p><p>Both candidates call for more guardrails on data center development, a topic that has been increasingly contentious across the state.</p><p>Melissa Mouritsen, a political science professor at the College of DuPage, says it’s understandable that Syed is attracting so much money from her party, which likely sees her as a rising star.</p><p>“Syed has done a good job of rallying the base,” Mouritsen says.</p><p>She adds that the Hills-Syed race appears to be one of the few competitive contests after a number of bruising primaries last March where most Democratic incumbents survived challenges from within their own party.  More than a quarter of the members of the Illinois General Assembly represent Chicago or portions of the city, and the vast majority are Democrats.</p><p></p><p>Only one incumbent Democrat lost in March. State Rep. Jaime Andrade Jr. was beat in his primary for House District 40 by challenger and community activist Miguel Alvelo Rivera for the North Side seat. Alvelo Rivera is unopposed in the November election. </p><p>While Democrats see a potential to pick up suburban seats — like in the Syed-Hills race — such gains likely only pad the big advantages they have in the legislature.</p><p>Democrats hold super-majorities in both the Illinois House (78-40) and Illinois Senate (40-19). Every Illinois House seat is up for election Nov. 3, while voters will decide 39 state senate races, two thirds of the total members.</p><p>Elsewhere, Democrats are hoping to unseat 52nd House District Republican Martin McLaughlin as he faces Maria Peterson again. In 2024, McLaughlin eked out a victory against Peterson, beating her by fewer than 50 votes.</p> <p>Peterson cites affordability, environmental protection and safety atop of the issues she's focusing on, and points to her records as a lawyer doing advocacy work.</p><p>"I’ve spent my life helping people navigate the systems that affect their lives, and I want to bring that same commitment to Springfield to lower costs, make government more responsive and serve the families of our community," she says.</p><p>McLaughlin says he’s focused on government spending and accountability as top issues.</p><p>“Property taxes remain one of the most significant concerns I hear from residents," he says. "My approach has been to focus on government spending, accountability and whether taxpayers are receiving value for the money they send to Springfield.”</p><p>Republicans also see opportunities. In another rematch, Republican Liz Bishop is challenging incumbent Democrat Amy “Murri” Briel in the 76th Illinois House District race in north central Illinois. The campaign includes some eyebrow-raising allegations.</p><p>Bishop, who lost to Briel in 2024 by less than 600 votes, released a recorded interview with a former staffer who alleged that Briel sexually harassed her, fed her prescription stimulant drugs and smoked pot while working as a lawmaker.</p><p>Briel denies the allegations and points to a state legislative watchdog investigation that concluded the claims were unfounded.</p><p>“It was an important story to tell,” Bishop says, adding that she believes her opponent is also out of touch with voters in the district. Briel didn't respond to requests for comment. </p><p>Closer to Chicago, state Sen. Emil Jones III faced a pair of challengers in the March primary after the District 14 incumbent faced federal corruption allegations. He won the election, getting more than 60% of the vote.</p><p>In November, Republican Brian Skala, a union plumber and elected official in Crestwood, hopes to oust Jones. </p><p>“People are talking about accountability and transparency,” he says. “Give us a chance to make it better.”</p>

entries.title: Chicago civil rights leader Al Raby is memorialized with a street dedication
entries.summary: <p>Katanya Raby said she didn’t know the late civil rights leader Al Raby as the “big, larger than life person that the rest of the city saw him as.”</p><p>“For me, Al Raby is my grandpa,” said Katanya Raby, CEO and co-founder of the Al Raby Foundation.</p><p>But to many, Al Raby is known for orchestrating a school boycott of nearly 300,000 students to protest school segregation in 1963, bringing Dr. Martin Luther King Jr. to Chicago in 1966 to protest poor housing conditions for Black Chicagoans, and serving as the campaign manager for Mayor Harold Washington’s historic 1983 election as the city’s first Black mayor.</p><p>On Friday, Al Raby’s legacy was memorialized with a street dedication and the proclamation of February 19, 2027 as Al Raby Day. While announcing the proclamation, Mayor Brandon Johnson encouraged Chicago residents to spend that day learning about Raby’s life and to build upon his legacy.</p><p>“I followed the example of Al Raby in demanding an education system that offers every child and every educator and every family a chance to succeed,” Johnson said.</p><p>More than 100 people filled the Grand Ballroom in Woodlawn as “golden oldies” of the 1960s boomed through speakers. Guests sat at round tables adorned with black cloth and decorated with “Al Raby Ln” cookies and round-lapel pins bearing his face.</p><p>Libations, an ancestral recognition ceremony, were offered by Pilar Audain, a Chicago-based healer and peacemaker. Then Chicago poet and author Leslé Honoré performed an original poem highlighting Raby’s life. Johnson and former Governor Pat Quinn offered remarks and reflections on Raby’s life, and Sherman ‘Dilla’ Thomas shared a mini-history lesson on Raby’s work on the school boycott.</p><p>The block-long stretch of Cottage Grove Ave. between 63rd and 64th streets is now Al Raby Lane. class="Figure-content"><figcaption class="Figure-caption"><p>In this file photo from Aug. 13, 1966, Al Raby, right, is pictured with Dr. Martin Luther King Jr., center, during a news conference. King said that Chicago Mayor Richard Daley could do more “to deal with problems we confront in the Negro community.” King asked for efforts to retain peace in the black Southwest Side where a disturbance started when police turned off a fire hydrant. </p></figcaption><span class="line"></span><div class="Figure-credit"><p>Charles Knoblock/Sun-Times Media</p></div></div> </figure> </div> </div><p>Raby’s organizing around Chicago public education was motivated by the conditions he witnessed as a teacher.</p><p>He had had enough of stuffing his students into the “Willis Wagons” and expecting them to learn. The wagons were mobile classrooms that then-Chicago Public Schools Supt. Benjamin C. Willis used to address overcrowding in majority-Black schools instead of allowing Black students to attend underutilized white schools. At the time, the district had yet to desegregate the schools to comply with the 1954 U.S. Supreme Court ruling of Brown v. Board of Education, which established that racialsegregation of public schools was unconstitutional.</p><p>In response, as leader of the Coordinating Council of Community Organizations, Raby organized what is known as “Freedom Day,” on October 22, 1963, a day when nearly 300,000 students, most of them Black, stayed home from school to protest segregation and the poor conditions in Black schools, and for the district to get rid of Willis.</p><p>Over the next 25 years, Raby would continue his civil rights work. In addition to his work with King and Washington, Raby ran the Peace Corps in Ghana, as it became a newly independent country during the Carter administration.</p><h3><b>History we can’t forget </b></h3><p>Katanya Raby said her grandfather practiced humility that drew people to him.</p><p>“It wasn’t about making himself the star of the show. It was about getting the work done,” she said. “He’s not listed on many of these organizations’ founding documents because that wasn’t his goal. His goal was to make sure that the organization could get off the ground.”</p><p>Because of the impact of their work, Katanya Raby says that the legacy of her grandfather and his contemporaries needs to be remembered.</p><p>“It’s important for us to preserve history of folks like my grandfather,” she said. “Black folks’ history, in these spaces, has really made a mark on the way the city looks, entries.title: Pope Leo leaves Rome’s Gemelli hospital 4 days after lung cancer surgery
entries.summary: <p>Pope Leo left Rome’s Gemelli hospital on Saturday, four days after undergoing surgery for lung cancer.</p><p>Dozens of well-wishers greeted the pope as he walked out of the hospital and into a waiting vehicle to return to the Vatican.</p><p>The 71-year-old pontiff had the lower lobe of his right lung removed after doctors identified a suspected cancerous nodule. The surgery confirmed <a class="Link" href="https://apnews.com/article/pope-leo-xiv-lung-cancer-adenocarcinoma-56b1c4fa87864d157eb3999a64f94c87" target="_blank" >he had adenocarcinoma</a>, the most common type of lung cancer.</p><p>His personal physician and surgeon said in a separate statement that Leo was “deemed fit for discharge from the hospital” based on blood test results and a chest X-ray performed Saturday morning, along with an assessment of his clinical condition.</p><p>He is set to leave the hospital in the early afternoon and return to the Vatican, the Vatican said in a brief statement.</p><p>With notable transparency, Leo announced last Sunday to the faithful gathered in St. Peter’s Square that doctors had identified a nodule on his lung, and that it would be removed.</p><p>Since the surgery on Tuesday that confirmed the cancer diagnosis, Leo has given strong indications that he was recovering well, including by holding a phone call with Russian President Vladimir Putin, meeting with top aides and celebrating Mass in a makeshift hospital chapel.</p><p>Medical bulletins from his personal physician and surgeon likewise indicated a good post-operative recovery that had allowed him to carry on “normal daily activities completely on his own.”</p><p>The Vatican on Friday released the first images of Leo since his surgery, showing him standing up at an altar in a hospital chapel in green vestments, as doctors said that tests confirmed his “continued improvement.”</p><p>Leo presided alone over the liturgy, distributing Communion to medical personnel and Vatican gendarmes present, Vatican spokesman Matteo Bruni said. He also delivered a homily in which he thanked the hospital staff “for the work they do every day taking care of the sick in their fragility, and in a particular way what they had done for him,” Bruni said.</p><p>The Vatican had originally estimated a weeklong hospital stay, and canceled his audiences through Tuesday. Experts indicated that patients could be discharged earlier depending on the pace of their recovery, and Bruni said the discharge date was up to the pope's doctors.</p><p>The pope’s next big agenda item is a trip to Latin America from Nov. 6-17, which gives Leo three more weeks of recovery before taking on the ambitious journey that includes a dozen flights and two helicopter trips.</p><p>The Vatican has given signs of all-systems go, publishing the names of journalists accredited to fly on Leo’s plane on Friday. And oncology surgeons say protocols generally clear patients to fly after three weeks, as long as recovery allows.</p><p>Doctors are still awaiting the results of tests to understand the precise molecular and genetic makeup of the cancer, whether it has spread beyond the lobe and whether any further treatment is necessary.</p>

entries.title: 4 men injured in Little Village drive-by shooting
entries.summary: <p>Four men were shot Friday night in Little Village on the Southwest Side. </p><p>The men were exiting a building in the 4000 block of West 26th Street when a vehicle drove by and someone inside opened fire around 11:15 p.m., Chicago police said. </p><p>One man, 56, was shot in the leg, while another, 26, was struck in the foot, police said. A third man, 25, was shot in the hand. </p><p>All three men were taken to Mount Sinai Hospital and are in good condition, police said. </p><p>A fourth man, 19, was shot in the arm and self-transported to Mount Sinai in good condition. </p><p>No arrests were made. </p>

entries.title: Bears activate CB Kyler Gordon
entries.summary: <p>Kyler Gordon, the slot cornerback whose months-long calf injury frustrated his bosses, will play Sunday against the Falcons.</p><p>Gordon was activated from the physically unable to perform list Saturday afternoon as the Bears left Halas Hall to fly to Atlanta. To make room, the Bears put defensive end Dayo Odeyingbo on injured reserve. Odeyingbo, who hurt his quad last week, will miss at least four games. The Bears also signed cornerback Nick McCloud to the active roster and cut safety Xavier Woods.</p><p>The Bears also promoted linebacker Buddy Johnson and running back Zavier Scott from the practice squad.</p><p>After he played only three regular season games last year because of various injuries, the Bears focused on Gordon getting healthy — and staying that way — this offseason. He was limited during their offseason program, however, and did not participate at all during training camp. On the eve of the regular season, general manager Ryan Poles said he couldn't guarantee that Gordon would play for the Bears during the season.</p><p>Gordon went outside Halas Hall as part of his calf rehab and began practicing with the team two weeks ago. The tone of the Bears' coaching staff changed soon thereafter. Before, Johnson was curt whenever answering any questions about Gordon.</p><p>"I think Kyler can help us win games," defensive coordinator Dennis Allen said Thursday. "When that time comes where he's able to be out there on the field and participate and help us win games, I'm looking forward to that time.”</p><p>Woods played 60% of the Bears' defensive snaps this season, starting twice.</p>
